utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you Madam. And good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I'm able to follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Jan Wubben. I'm the lead counsel for the Prosecution together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And also good morning to you Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. And good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, my colleagues from the Prosecution. I am Vasvija Vidovic together with Mr. John Jones. I'm the Defence counsel for Mr. Naser Oric. Together with us are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic and Ms. Adisa Mehic and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. My apologies to you I didn't realise --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think there is a preliminary, which the Prosecution might need to elaborate themselves on. But basically, we filed an exhibit list a few days ago concerning the exhibits we intend to use with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Some of them have a prefix R, which as I learnt for the first time relates to Rule 70 material. The exhibits which we intend to use were all disclosed to us by the Prosecution. I have the receipts and the dates, if need be. Yesterday I was alerted to the fact that the Prosecution perhaps was still needing to secure certain clearances in order for that material to, I suppose, enter the public domain and for that reason I delayed using them yesterday. I've received this morning a list indicating which of the documents received clearance and which haven't. There are still some which haven't and which, of course, I would like to use. What I propose doing is, I can shift those exhibits to tomorrow so that in the meantime I understand the Prosecution is still seeking clearances and then perhaps we'll end up finishing a bit early today but then that can be dealt with tomorrow. I should say that our position is that we've received these documents, they were disclosed to us without any indication that they were confidential or anything of that nature. We do intend to use them. If need be, some expedience such as sitting in closed session or filing the exhibits under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sitting in closed session doesn't solve the problem, in Rule 70 material. If it comes to the worst, then the only solution that there is, Mr. Jones, is that fortunately you are aware of the contents. You can make use of the contents without referring to the specific document. And proceed accordingly, but there is no other way. Do I take it, Mr. Wubben or Mr. Di Fazio, I don't know who is handling this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, but that basically you are in the process of receiving clearances from the sources that are Rule 70 protected?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The situation is that these were handed over to the Prosecution some time ago. I wanted to satisfy myself that they were -- clearance had been received, put matters into train to make that enquiry. We're still awaiting that notification. There is every possibility that clearance will be provided; however, we are yet to receive it. And I'm grateful to Mr. Jones for being so accommodating and agreeing to rearrange, in effect, his cross-examination so that he can extend more time to the Prosecution to make those enquiries and hopefully get to the bottom of the matter as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, the -- okay, I thank you for that information, Mr. Di Fazio. Now I draw your attention to Rule 70(B), please. "If the Prosecution is in possession of information which has been provided to the Prosecutor on a confidential basis and which has been used solely for the purpose of generating new evidence, that initial information and its origin shall not be disclosed by the Prosecutor without the consent of the person or entity providing the initial information. And shall in any event not be given in evidence without prior disclosure to the accused." Now, I take it that if the accused or Defence are already in possession of these documents, that presumes that there has been clearance already from whoever gave you the documents in confidence. Am I correct, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You are correct and that would be in the normal course of events, and I hope and expect that we will eventually find the source of the clearance for these particular documents that Mr. Jones is talking about. The problem that the Prosecution has is essentially a record keeping one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What we have is, I can't -- when I found the documents, I said, where is the clearance for this material? I want to be satisfied about it so that I, myself, might be able to use the documents. And matters were put -- enquiries were started and it's the inability to find that clearance that is the source of the problem in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. That makes me less optimistic, as I was when I started speaking. Let's wait a bit, Mr. Jones, and see how this develops and then we will take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it if you have them, it's either because the Prosecution has made a humungous mistake by disclosing to them to you without clearance or else because there has effectively been clearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That's why our position is ultimately we should be able to use them, but we're prepared to desist in using them for a period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And there may be a certain amount of shuffling of exhibits, a certain amount of wielding that we will have to do on our side, so I trust you will bear with us because it affects the order on which I was going to present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously. Obviously. But I take it I have your word, Mr. Di Fazio, that there is someone actively engaged in trying to take this clearance up, wherever it may be?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: They're very, very busy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Otherwise there will be guillotines in place in this courtroom later on in the day. Yes, I'm making it clear. Yes, Madam Usher, can you escort the witness, please. In the meantime, Mr. Jones, if you want to make use of the contents, once you have the documents, the presumption is that they have been handed to you, the legal presumption is that they have been handed to you legally, in a legal fashion, and I suppose you can easily, without any problems at all, make use of that information, not necessarily of the document. In other words, for the time being, until we clear this up, I don't think I can authorise you to say, there is this document released by, or provided by -- which states the following. You can put to the witness the contents or the substance of the contents, of those documents that you are interested in, without indicating or giving an indication to the witness what document or what source you are relying upon or that document relies upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you can move along in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Where possible, I will try to distill a proposition from the document and put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, if you could do that. I mean obviously but, otherwise, the presumption has to be that you have them legitimately and you have come into possession of them in a legitimate manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Please take a seat and we are going to proceed with the cross-examination. Again, I'm sorry we called you about 12 minutes late, but, as usual, we start every morning here with problems, be they technical or procedural or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, please you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Colonel Tucker. I hope you are well rested.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: A general question before we go back to the diary, because we haven't with that yet. I'm going to deliberately go very slowly today for the interpreters. I trust you will bear with me. You described yesterday some pretty disturbing matters, people getting in knife fights over the food and air drops, people not having food in Srebrenica for days on end. People sleeping out on the streets, freezing cold. Are you still troubled by your memories from your stay in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You were there for a little over two weeks; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And to the many months that other people, including our client was present in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I also want to deal with a matter I touched on yesterday, but without having the exhibit in front of me, you will recall I referred to Philip Morillon's book 'Croire et Oser'. And, in fact, I will pass up copies of that exhibit now, the relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did he write his book in English or in French?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In French. Has it been translated into English?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies, it hasn't. I was working on the basis that the working languages of the court were English and French and I'm hoping the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I understand French, I'm just curious whether there is such an important book as this has been translated into French by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry has the book been translated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the book, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't believe so but I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now if I could direct your attention firstly to page 165. You will see at the bottom of the second paragraph, where there is the reference to the famous quote, "Je n'ai pas senti l'odeur de la mort". I didn't smell the odour of death.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And that refers to what General Morillon said when he went to Cerska?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, if I could read the next passage, and I will do the best with my school boy French. [French spoken]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I don't know what's happening. Of course I could follow you in French. But although Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and myself are the ones who ought to follow most, there are others also who need to follow what is being said and I did not receive interpretation. So I take it that there was no interpretation to the outside world or to whoever doesn't understand French.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is asking whether Mr. Jones wouldn't mind repeating because French was not -- you know scheduled, scheduled. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So what we will do, Madam Usher, could I ask you, please, to put this on the ELMO, page 165.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps I should suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the penultimate paragraph. Penultimate paragraph, page 165.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If in fact given Colonel Tucker's French is no doubt much better than mine, perhaps, you wouldn't mind reading that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was little to say, that there hadn't been any dead in this battle, including innocent civilians, victims of the bombing. I meant to say that there had been no massacre. My duty was to have to try and calm or reduce hatred and try to favour peace first in the minds.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Isn't it correct to say when General Morillon made that comment he wasn't saying there hadn't been deaths of innocent civilians, he was only saying he hadn't seen evidence of a massacre?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And is it also your understanding that he partly down played the scale of the crisis as reflected in that paragraph, because he felt it was his role to calm down hatred and animosity?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was his role to calm down hatred and animosity, but that was by telling the truth. And he did not see, in what he saw, in other words, he did not see what he did not see. He had no evidence that convinced him that a massacre or massacres had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: It's true isn't it, that on that day, General Morillon only saw a very small part of Cerska and he didn't go in the outlying areas?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What General Morillon told me when he returned from Cerska was that he and his party had only walked in and around the buildings of the village of Cerska and had not gone up into the hills or into the woods of the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what date would this be? What --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 6th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 6th of March. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, turning the page, on page 166, there's a section dealing with Konjevic Polje. Again, if I could ask you just to read the first paragraph in French and if the booth could interpret that into English.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the top page of 166, from -- [Interpretation] I learned then that the Serbs had not stopped their offensive and that following Cerska, they bombed Konjevic -- [No Interpretation] Sorry, I'm hearing the translation simultaneously in my ear and it is very confusing to read. I will start again. [Interpretation] I learned then that the Serbs had not stopped their offensive and that following Cerska they had bombed Konjevic Polje, driving the inhabitants under the horrified gaze of the blue helmets and Abraham saw women and children die. He saw his own vehicles being hit, some of them destroyed, and he had to withdraw on orders with the inhabitants fleeing into the mountains, taking away their wounded because there was nothing else to -- left to be done on this part.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. And does that passage reflect your understanding of what happened in Konjevic Polje after General Morillon left? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, this would be, what day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- where he talks about the bombardment of Konjevic Polje, that would have been after the 6th of March. I had no hard information as to when that happened. It was only when we were in Srebrenica, on the 11th and 12th of March, that we were told that that had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you look at the next page on page 167, in fact, there is the third paragraph, J'arrive le dix mars. So, it had to be between the 6th and 10th in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We can probably fix the date with other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. But I just asked in case the witness could pinpoint that. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Yes, so subsequently, did you understand that that is in fact what had happened?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And just three more passages, if you could please read the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was then convinced that the Serbs, despite what they promised, were resolved and determined to clean up the area of any Muslim presence up to the end in the area. Paris shares this analysis. I talked about it with general Wahlgren in Zagreb and I told him I feared that Srebrenica would very soon have the same fate as Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And then just before I ask you about that, if we could just see the next paragraph on page 167. If you could please read that finally.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one starting -- [Interpretation] Refugees, most of them are women and children, flow in the tens of thousands. They live on the street without any shelter. Srebrenica is an impasse from which they cannot escape. The weakest start dying of hunger. Any attack on their city will be a catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And do those reflections reflect what you believed as well at the time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And finally, on page 171, in the penultimate paragraph, there's a mention of Philip von Recklinghausen who you mentioned. You also mentioned Tony Birtley. Do you know who Tony -- did you know who Tony Birtley was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tony Birtley was a UK national. He was a free-lance reporter, at that stage working for ITV, not BBC.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And the last sentence there says: [Interpretation] He confirmed what we saw as soon as we arrived. Srebrenica is hell. [No Interpretation] And do you share that opinion?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I would ask if this document could be given an exhibit number, this extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Jones. This will become --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D217.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to take you back to the diary now, so if you could have that in front of you. Thanks. I forget which exhibit number it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'm just reminded, we do have the issue of -- still of how the diary will be dealt with, the issue which Your Honour mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you notice, you may have noticed yesterday, I did not raise the matter again. I was waiting to see how deep into it both of you would have bitten and then I would have put the question at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay, we can proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the only way of going about it. I will not make any further pronouncements in the course of cross-examination for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have a position, and I can state that in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Colonel, if you could turn to page 3456, please, which is where we left off. Okay. Just to reorient ourselves, this is the 14th of March and you read paragraph A, the bottom half. If you could now just, please, read B and C.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people believe they will be killed in the next few weeks. The Serb offensive is alleged to have started 10 days ago and would appear to be relentless to eating the enclave up village by village. It is not a quick three-day attack. Serb aircraft from Serbia are confirmed as supporting these attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your source for this intelligence?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part?

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: The Serb offensive is alleged to have started ten days ago?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that by the -- by members of the War Presidency and that we'd been told that earlier in Konjevic Polje by Colonel Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Was it that this intensified offensive had started ten days before?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, when I was in Zvornik later in Major Pandurovic's office, he had taken us into that office and up on the wall was a map which showed the boundaries of his forces, his force's front line, on a series of dates. And, in fact, the start date of that offensive was the 7th of February. But I did not know that at the time that this was written.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So that you had information that, in fact, the offensive might have started considerably earlier than ten days before the 14th of March?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I only had that information subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: As far as the offensive which was going on while you were in Srebrenica, do you have any estimate of how many people were killed by Serb shelling in the town of Srebrenica during that time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in Srebrenica, there was negligible shelling of Srebrenica and the town. The United Nations military observers, who had been south of Srebrenica, they had themselves seen and witnessed shelling of outlying villages, which were at the edge of the Srebrenica enclave in the way that I had described yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And were they reporting major casualties?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were reporting numbers of casualties, but not in -- not major numbers of casualties. We were far more concerned about people -- refugees dying of starvation, because the refugees were uprooted and only had any food that they could carry. We were told that many of them had been on the march for about five days and they had not eaten in five days. Shelling was, as I had described yesterday, which was sporadic, three shells an hour into a village. That's not going to cause large numbers of casualties but it is sure going to terrify the population. The other reason for the refugees being in dire need of food and being starving is that the inhabitants -- the local inhabitants of Srebrenica and the War Presidency appeared to be doing nothing to actually help the refugees. The people, the inhabitants of Srebrenica had stocks of food, but which they were, I suppose understandably, keeping for themselves, they were not making anything available to the refugees. It was the refugees who were our main concern in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And in that regard, when you touched on that subject yesterday, I think you also said that soldiers hadn't helped. I want to ask you a question or two about the concept of soldiers in Bosnia, because you also told us that even someone in a uniform with a weapon wasn't necessarily indicative that they were a soldier. First, would you accept that, that that's not indicative?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The definition of soldier, as is understood in a democratic country in Bosnia is not particularly relevant. The male population of Bosnia provided they were more than 19, 20 years old, will probably have had their national service and therefore know how to use a weapon. So therefore every male within Bosnia who is more than 20 can hold weapons and understand the basics of military tactics. That does not mean they are soldiers, though, and if they are attacked, then anyone will grab whatever weapon they have available to try and defend themselves. The issue of soldiers is to what extent they were organised in and subject to military command and subject to military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a very helpful definition. Applying that definition, when during your testimony you've referred to soldiers in Srebrenica, isn't it right that in fact you're not able to say whether they fit into that conventional definition of belonging to a hierarchy? You're speaking of someone who may have been in a uniform or been able-bodied; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I refer to soldiers, what I'm referring to are people who were visibly following orders and acting in an organised and controlled manner, as opposed to many of the people in Srebrenica, refugees who were wearing bits of military uniform simply because they were good heavy and warm, that did not mean they were necessarily soldiers. When I refer to soldiers, I mean people who were following orders and who were acting in an organised and controlled way.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Sergeant you don't speak or you didn't speak at the time Serbo-Croatian as it was known?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So when you talk about people visibly following orders, you weren't actually hearing orders being issued in and around the town, were you? That's an inference.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To give specific examples, when we arrived in Konjevic Polje, and we were escorted by a couple of Colonel Oric's officers and a couple of what I took to be bodyguards, Colonel Oric spoke to them and they then went away and did things and they came back and they said things. Now, what was said, I can't comment on. Similarly, in and around the PTT building, there were soldiers who were guarding the place, both downstairs at the front entrance and upstairs, the radio room and the meeting room and for a couple of days when we were in that -- that other room in the top floor. It was clear, I mean you don't need to understand the language, to be able to see that there is somebody giving orders and there is somebody else who is receiving them and following instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So you're inferring on the basis of someone speaking to someone, someone going off and coming back and saying something in some cases you're inferring an order being issued on that basis?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is one further basis and that is Mihailov, who speaks Serbo-Croat and he was an important source to me of information locally about what was going on and who was saying what to who, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to belabour the subject, but I put it to you, on certain occasions anyway, some occasions when you inferred an order from that behavior, it was simply people exchanging information and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, if the witness has already said he didn't understand the language and this Mihailov was there to tell him, he can't comment on what was transpiring between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's classic case of the counsel now speculating instead of the witness. Move to the next question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If we can go back to the diary, 3457 is the next page. And we have airdrop sitrep: 6 aircraft dropped just north of Srebrenica, population fighting over bundles, three to six people killed during each drop. Now at this stage, were these still pallets which were falling or were they MREs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were pallets of MREs.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you see each night or many nights when you were in Srebrenica, a spectacle of many, many people from Srebrenica going out to the hills at night to await the airdrops, burning fires on the hills and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What would happen is that, as it started getting dark, the refugees who were all scattered around the PTT building -- as I described previously -- would slowly head north and the place would empty and there would be hardly anyone left because they had all gone up to where the drop sites were. And then during the night they -- after the drops, they would slowly drift back. It took about an hour and a half, two hours walk to get from the PTT building up to the drop sites, above the town.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: During this -- during these events, would you hear shots being fired from the -- from that direction?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The odd shot, burst of machine-gun fire.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You've gone into this in some detail yesterday, but would it be fair to summarise, this as a fight for survival -- struggle for survival, in which the fittest were basically getting their hands on the food, basically, in which the law of the jungle prevailed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you touched on something that was of considerable concern to us. It was the strongest and fittest who were getting the food, not the weakest, who actually needed it. And that's a recurring concern that we had and that the War Presidency did not appear to be doing very much to gather food and make sure the weak women and children actually got it rather than the strong.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Did they ever tell you there was very little they could do?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They never made that excuse. I think that they were so demoralised that even the basics that they could have done, they weren't doing. It was only when Larry Hollingsworth, the UNHCR person who was with us, he actually organised them and showed them how to set up a refugee reception centre and an accommodation unit to actually move refugees in an organised way into empty unused buildings and so on, and to organise the collection of food that was dropped in order that -- and as time went on, and their morale improved, they started getting a bit better at that.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could turn to the next page, 3458. I'm looking at the very bottom that goes into 3459. It's the comment "Serbs furious that there are some UNMOs in", I think it is "Sreb". Is it correct that the Serbs -- you understood that the Serbs, firstly, were furious that there were United Nations military observers in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs were furious and we know that because we had a report from a meeting between some UNMOs and General Milovanovic at the silver mine, at the entrance to the route that we had come in. And he had been furious with his local commander for letting us go past that route. Secondly, is Milovanovic, when we met him at the yellow bridge, said that there was no agreement for military observers to be deployed into Srebrenica and that you, General Morillon, had just taken them in without the approval of the Serb -- Bosnian Serb Assembly. And it was returned to in most meetings that we had with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Aside from that slightly bureaucratic explanation which they gave, was it your opinion that, in fact, the Serbs didn't want the outside world to know what was going on in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If you can skip forward to 3463 and that's 15th of March. The Prosecution asked about this page and the next couple of pages. And there's the reference, which I think was read out, to shelling and bombing at a low rate until arrival. But then reference to cluster bomb casings and 128-millimetre rocket mortars. Motors.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Motors. It's the only thing that is left over from 128-millimetre rocket when it explodes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So as an artillery officer, you would be familiar with both of these weapons. Can you tell us a lit bit about cluster bombs, first of all?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A cluster bomb is a fairly new type of weapon which is a package containing many small bombs about 700 or 750 of them. And when the bomb is dropped, when it is a short distance above the ground, a small explosive charge scatters these many -- think of them as little hand grenades which then independently explode. Cluster bombs are for use against infantry and personnel in the open. They are not any use against armoured vehicles or buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So is it right that there can be a pretty devastating effect of cluster bombs being dropped on a civilian population?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We found a cluster bomb casing in the south of the main part of the town and we could see where the -- all the little bomblet's had exploded, had scarred a couple of apartment blocks. In other words, this cluster bomb had been dropped on a city of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: An then 128-millimetre calibre, that's a very large calibre, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that large a calibre, but it's a -- it's a rocket of a multiple rocket-launch system. So it's not individual rockets. It's these batteries of them. And they just fire very quickly, one after the other. And again, it is an area weapon for use against soft targets, people. It is not really that much use against armoured vehicles or buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And these weapons -- taking, first of all, the multiple rocket launcher, these were weapons of the JNA, which the Bosnian Serb army had inherited. Would that be your understanding?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And you mentioned armoured vehicles. The fact is the Bosnians didn't have any armoured vehicles, did they, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one tank. There was one T55 tank which we were told had no fuel, available fuel. They captured and it was in the middle of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: It was captured from the Serb?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was captured from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If you turn to the next page, you were also asked about these groupings in the area. Page 3464. In fact, I withdraw that, that's been dealt with, I think, thoroughly yesterday. So we will move on from that page to 3467. Again, this is the 15th of March, I think you will agree.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And this is your note, isn't it, of a meeting between General Morillon, General Milovanovic and a third person.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Tolimir, Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And these are all officers of the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Then with the line after it, which looks to be like a J, represents what General Morillon said?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is M and a bracket.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Near the top there, he appears to be saying: "Propose to solve your problem by demil area, deploy," I suppose that refers to the Canadian company.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What he was proposing was to solve your, as in the Serb problem, by demilitarising the area and by deploying a Canadian company.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And that would solve the Serbs problem because the Muslims wouldn't be fighting anymore?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims wouldn't be carrying out the attacks on the Serbs, Serb civilians, that they were getting so angry about and were using as their excuse for continuing their offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You confirmed, haven't you, you're not aware -- you don't actually know where Serb civilians were ever targeted by --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge and was not shown any such information. We were taken to Kravica and were told of things, but we were not in a position to confirm or deny anything.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: All right. If we turn to the next page, 3468. This is still General Morillon speaking. We've got two sentences, lines -- actually, we can -- it's the numbers on the side, lines 9 to 11, "deploy UN soldiers to demilitarised area, like" --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Status of UNPA in Krajina, police and UN soldiers only allowed in the area." General Morillon was making an analogy to the situation in the Krajina UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: When he refers to police, that would be civilian Bosniak police; would that be right? Was that the understanding?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My understanding is that it was police of either side, but not soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Not military police?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not military police.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now if we go a bit further down, you have line 16 to 18, "I know you wished to clean out this nest of terrorists. I will do it for you and save you many, many casualties".

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: That's General Morillon speaking to the Serbs and referring to Srebrenica as the nest of terrorists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was speaking in language that the Serbs would understand. That was the language which the Serbs had been using for General Morillon to refer to them, otherwise would have been difficult in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words speaking a language that the Serbs would digest better, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was repeating back to the Serbs the things that they had been saying to him.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You will forgive me if I dwell on this, but it may go to the attitude of the Bosnian towards General Morillon and the United Nations when we see that phrase. General Morillon had been in the enclave for three days at this point, I suppose, is that about right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about that.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: He had seen the suffering which you had seen, the women and children starving, people on the streets. Was that really good practice of him to refer to Srebrenica as a nest of terrorists?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sat here, I can understand why you raise more than an eyebrow. Where we were, the situation was desperate and what General Morillon wanted was to achieve the objectives that we've been through before. The Serbs were highly excited, very angry, much more angry than we had seen them in the previous three months that -- four months that we had been in Bosnia. And they were absolutely determined that these were terrorists and they were going to sort them out. And what General Morillon wanted to do was to calm them down and so he was using language that he did not believe, but that in the conversation there, then, in the heat of the moment, there then is what I wrote down, I recorded, as to what General Morillon said. What I categorically refute is that General Morillon considered the Bosniaks in Srebrenica all to be terrorists. He was using the language which had been used, shouted at him by the Serbs. Please do not take this out of the context that this actually occurred in.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I want to examine the context a bit more, because it follows from that, doesn't it, that the Serbs were furious against the enclave, considered the people there terrorists and they were bent on some sort of revenge; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Revenge was the word uppermost in my mind as to what the Serbs were after. There was continual complaint about war criminals in the pockets and whenever we talked about evacuation of injured, the caveat from the Serbs was always: the women and children, fine; the men, not. The men, we want to search and check against lists that they claimed they had of war criminals and that those who they claimed were war criminals, they would take off to and put through their legal system.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: In this climate, did you and General Morillon consider that if the Muslims were disarmed, there was a grave risk that there would be an appalling massacre, at this time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is why General Morillon was so adamant about the introduction of UN military observers, because without UN military observers, it was impossible for there to be any kind of guarantees of anything and exactly the issue you describe was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: But when you speak of UNMOs, we're talking about half a dozen or a dozen individuals observing a situation. Surely more than that is required to defend the enclave against possible attack.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Morillon had, by that stage, already issued orders for 36 UNMOs to be deployed and to be prepared for deployment. He had four with them and there were a further four who followed shortly behind, the ones who bumped into Milovanovic at the silver mine. These are to observe a cease-fire. This is not in any way shape or form a defensive force able to protect in military action.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And what was the estimate for the size of the defensive force which would be required?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made no plans at that time about a defensive force. General Morillon was talking about deploying the Canadian battalion which was held up at Zvornik, into Srebrenica. And shortly after I left, they made arrangements, in fact for a company of them to deploy into the -- into Srebrenica. While I was there, the focus of effort was on getting UNMOs -- UN military observers deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And accompanying which was deployed which was what, between 100, 150?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Typically a Canadian company, about 150 men.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And are you aware that subsequently, when it came to estimating how many soldiers would be needed to protect the enclave, that was considered a woefully inadequate number, that many, many companies would be required?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were going to protect the enclave, you would have needed four, six, 8000 soldiers; not the kind of numbers we're talking here. And General Morillon had nothing like that resource available. There was nothing like that resource going to be available in the near future. What there was available and what could be deployed quickly was UN military observers and that is why he focussed on that.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that nothing like 8000 soldiers, UN soldiers were ever deployed to defend the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. My understanding that is purely from reading the media is that DutchBat was about 600 or so. But at no stage was that ever a credible defensive force.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were talking about Naser Oric's attitude to the proposal to demilitarise the enclave and, of course, we're not here to judge him for being a hawk or a dove.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: But did you -- I take what you said yesterday as not being a criticism of him, that he was contemplating fighting to the very end in and among the buildings as an alternative to demilitarising.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that Colonel Oric has far more and far worse experience of the Serbs than I do, and I can understand why he did not want to consider demilitarisation, that he was very anxious about what the risks that that incurred and General Morillon and I were very aware that there were risks.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: But despite his opposition, he was, in fact, overruled, wasn't he, in the sense that there was a demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened after I left.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, 3469, it's a matter I am going to come back to. But at line 15, there's reference "murder Turajlic". Do you see that? I will ask you --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Line 15?

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: "Murder Turajlic".

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, as I said, I will come back to this and it's with regard to the attitude that the Bosnian towards United Nations, but doesn't that refer to the murder of the Bosnian vice prime minister when in the custody of the United Nations near the airport? Murder by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Though the way that events were portrayed there, the way it actually happened, there are differences. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I believe you were involved in discussions as to whether this should be, or you and General Morillon, as to whether there should be an investigation into the responsibility of the French Colonel for that incident?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an investigation. It was carried out by General Valgon, in fact. And it lasted for about three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: But the perpetrator wasn't convicted, wasn't he, because immunity was granted to UN witnesses against testifying?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The perpetrator was a young Serb soldier who was identified by General Mladic. The Serbs refused to hand him over. General Mladic claimed that the Serb soldier had been court-martialled and punished. I have absolutely no way of confirming whether or not -- whether or not that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. We will come back to that with documents in due course. Now if you go to 3474. Again, I'm just looking towards the bottom where General Morillon appears to be saying -- perhaps you could read those three lines, something "I departed government of -- I deprived you of military victory". Could you read those three lines?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From which number?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And line number?

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: It would be 21 to 23.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Morillon: I deprived you of military victory. It would have been a real catastrophe to your cause". This is General Morillon saying to the Serbs. I think this is still the Milovanovic meeting, that he, General Morillon, by going into Srebrenica had deprived the Serbs of a military victory on the ground in Srebrenica and saying that: "If you, the Bosnian Serbs, had a military victory on the ground, it would have been a catastrophe, a diplomatically -- politically to your cause".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And do you know what General Morillon meant when he referred to "your cause"? What did you understand to be the Serbs cause?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb's cause, my understanding of the Serb's cause -- I can't comment on what General Morillon thought at that instant when he said that -- was the establishment of a independent Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Carved out of the --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb republic, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Which would break away from the United Nation's recognised republic of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which was part of, at that moment in time, international recognised single entity of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So as a representative of the United Nations, is it really correct that General Morillon was seeming to endorse the dismemberment of the United Nations' member state?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, the what -- witness has made quite clear, he said that he can't comment on what was going through General Morillon's mind at that particular time. And as I understand what has transpired in the questions and answers thereafter, the witness's views about what was happening at that particular time. Now, if that's relevant so be it. But I thought that the enquiry was what was going through General Morillon's mind and the meaning of that answer, at 3474. Now if we can get some insight into that of course I have no objection and the witness may be able to provide that insight. But the way the questions have developed so -- from that point onwards appear to be Colonel Tucker's views. And if you regard that as appropriate, then so be it. But we must be clear about the views that are being expressed being Colonel Tucker's views, because he said that he didn't understand -- or didn't know what was going through General Morillon's mind at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You would have been completely right, Mr. Di Fazio, had the question been: Would you agree that General Morillon was actually endorsing the dismemberment of the United Nations member state of BiH. But the question isn't that. The question was, is it really correct -- really correct, and pay attention to the words used by Mr. Jones, please, because I think this is a very carefully studied question. Is it really correct that General Morillon was seemingly endorsing or seeming to endorse ... In other words in his dealing with General Milovanovic -- or whatever his name is --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps I misread it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- was General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Giving the impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Giving the impression that he was sort of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps I jumped the gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sympathetic or whatever, which I think this being essentially a process of negotiations that was ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- at the time. I think the witness can easily, without any problems at all, answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Understood in that light, I have no objection to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't go to negotiate and the first thing you do is antagonise the person you are trying to negotiate with. In fact you try to show as much sympathy as possible with his or her cause, even if you are at heart miles away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand that. As I said understood in that light, then I've got no problem with the -- with the line of enquiry. I just want to be absolutely sure that everyone is clear about what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But of course he can answer the question. The question is certainly not: "What did General Morillon inwardly feel about the Serbian cause." That's not the question. I wouldn't let him answer it in any case, if that had been the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. My fears are allayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Jones, would you like us to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. It's your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: In this meeting, did General Morillon give the impression that he was sympathetic to the cause of dismembering a member state of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Not in this meeting nor in any other. He merely recognised that, as the judge said, people who are negotiating with had different points of view and their cause was their point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about cease-fires and the general policy of cease-fires and I'm coming at that subject to get at this topic. Isn't it correct that in the early months of the war, the Serbs seized something like 90 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina by violent ethnic cleansing operation, expelling Muslims from their homes?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the percentage of 90 is a substantial overstatement. But, yes, they did take a majority of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: What percentage would you estimate?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: About sixty.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it right that at this stage - we're talking about March, 1993 and even a bit before - that cease-fires were basically consolidate the status quo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Did you -- sorry you were going to add something?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our view that from April through to November, the Bosnian Serbs had carried out a deliberately planned policy of occupation and ethnic cleansing and that from the end of November, they believed, by their perverted logic, that they had seized all the territory that they, to their perverted logic, had a right to. And that's the reason, incidentally, why the front line, the confrontation line was such a militarily illogical line, if you were intending to defend something. And that from December 1992 onwards, the single intention of the Bosnian Serb military was to consolidate what they had taken and get the territory that they had taken recognised to get Republika Srpska recognised. And what they wanted was a cease-fire throughout all of Bosnia and for the fighting to stop, with them holding what they had taken.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So when you the met with Bosnian, Bosnian government representatives, did you detect sometimes a certain skepticism about your talk of cease-fires, given that it would consolidate that invidious position?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The situation was more complex than that. The -- it was our perception and by our perception I mean it was the headquarters' perception that the Bosniaks did not want to accept the status quo which had been forced upon them by superior military force, by the Bosnian Serbs and that they were, therefore, going to carry out military action as and where they could in order to try and reverse that situation. And what they never wanted to do was allow or give recognition of the current status. Now, in their military actions that they carried out, invariably the Serbs had more heavy weapons, but not very many infantry. And the typical course of events was that the Bosniaks would carry out an attack, somewhere. That it would make initial advances and have initial success because the Serbs did not have many soldiers, did not have many infantry. The Serbs would then use heavy weapons, tanks, artillery, and so on to repulse the attack and regain the territory which the Bosniaks had initially gained and would then carry out a punishment shelling of the area from where the attack had come in order to try and deter the Bosniaks from carrying out future attacks. Now of course the Bosniaks did not want to accept that, because they felt that they had lost territory which they wished to regain. Now when things started getting bad for the Bosniaks, because the Serb military superiority of force was giving the Serbs the advantage, that was when the Bosniaks then requested cease-fires and were requesting support by the United Nations, by General Morillon, for cease-fires. So General Morillon was going into - and this is not just General Morillon, this is all people in the UN in Bosnia at that time - were going into negotiations. They were requesting cease-fires in areas where things were going badly for the Bosniaks and the Serbs were saying: But the -- you, United Nations, are only acting as a tool for the Bosniaks and arranging cease-fires to prevent us from reversing a military situation. And what we, the Serbs want, is a ceasefire across all of Bosnia, not just in one convenient place so that the Bosniaks can carry out a tactical regrouping, bring up more men, bring up more ammunition and then start fighting again. 20

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So this pattern of what you described as raids on the Bosniak side, that's very much part of the whole military strategic position in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was exactly that. And it was of -- I described the situation where, from April through to November, it had been a battle of con quest by the Serbs, but the Serbs had then sat down and said we've taken what we need to take. It is our belief, from intelligence, et cetera, that the Bosniaks, seeing the Serbs ceasing their attacks and further seizure of territory, believed, mistakenly, that the - that the Serb military had overstretched themselves, had overreached themselves. And they then ordered a series of counter attacks. Those counter attacks started in Sarajevo, at the beginning of December, where they had a twin-pronged attack from Mount Igman and from Stup around the side of Sarajevo airport. That attack resulted in some of the heaviest fighting around Sarajevo that had ever taken place and resulted in the loss of most of Stup to the Bosnian Serbs and was some very vicious fighting. When we started seeing, in the international media in January, reports of an offensive in the eastern enclaves from the inside of the enclaves outwards and reports of Bosniak forces having even attacked across the river Drina and actually held some territory in Serbia itself for a while, this was considered to be further attempts by the Bosniak Presidency to move on to the offensive. However, they had gravely misjudged the force and the power that the Bosnian Serbs had available. They had believed that the Bosnian Serbs were -- had overstretched themselves. In fact they had simply stopped because they had taken what they believed was correct. Now, the Bosnian Serbs had misjudged the Muslims, the - sorry, the Bosniaks - resoluteness and they were surprised, they were taken by surprise by the -- they had not expected these attacks. And it took them until the 7th of February to organise themselves in the eastern enclaves in order to start their counter offensive, which then began as what I described as the Pacman-style attack of slowly but remorselessly village by village, but not in a massive way so the international community would then see a big bombardment or anything, but they would slowly, remorselessly eat into the enclaves for a number of reasons: For revenge, for what they claimed was the murders of Serb civilians of which had taken place, and the anger that the Serbs showed about that was much more than the excuses you described yesterday, weren't those kind of excuses used everywhere, yes, they were used everywhere, but in -- but in respect of Srebrenica they were really, really angry. I mean there was a difference in the anger that the Serbs had. Secondly, there was also the logistic resupply issue that I described with the map yesterday, and --

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I would like to come to that issue, if I can stop you there because that's a very, very full answer. I'm going to take a few points just briefly arising from what you've -- what you've said. You've said that one of the motives for the Serbs' remorseless attack on Srebrenica was revenge. I put it to you that there was a much more simple reason for it, which was that the enclaves were extremely inconvenient to the Serbs and they needed to be extinguished because they were in eastern Bosnia and they were a nuisance.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would entirely agree that there were -- there was that reason as well, but there were two reasons. There was what I would describe as the military logistic reason, but there was also this -- this revenge issue, which came up again and again.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, taking the logistic resupply issue -- first of all Sarajevo - obvious point - was under siege at this point. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And what you've described as attacks coming out of Sarajevo could also be described as attempts to break the siege?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was describing earlier, actually yesterday or the day before, was attacks from north of Sarajevo. In other words I -- when I showed you on the map the corridor from the sides, the flanks of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You can break the siege from the outside as well as from the inside? Can't you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now this logistic resupply issue -- I won't deal with the map now, but is it correct that the Serbs' complaint was essentially we're having difficulty in maintaining our siege of Sarajevo because our logistics route from Zvornik to Pale is being disrupted.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And Colonel Oric was making it very difficult for them.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So I hope this doesn't come across as flippant, but the poor old Serbs had to run a gauntlet in order to keep up the siege of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. Karadzic, in a meeting in the middle of February, after a meeting with General Morillon, took General Morillon aside and asked if he could help with a personal matter and said that a nephew of his had left Zvornik, a few days previously in a car, with four other people from Zvornik to go to Pale but had never arrived in Pale. Could General Morillon enquire with the Presidency forces whether they had any knowledge of what might have happened. And we enquired and we never found anything.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. Well, when I said the "poor Serbs", I was being ironic. Isn't it right that the siege of Sarajevo involved terrible sniping and shelling and killing of many, many innocent people?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: But were you, as the United Nations, listening to this complaint by the Serbs, they were having trouble keeping up the siege, this is a serious complaint?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not -- I never described it and it was not -- it was never described to us by the Serbs as "they were having difficulty keeping up the siege". It was making things difficult for them.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, I will talk for a moment on the subject, although I mean to come back to it. But I put it to you, what emerges from this is such a moral or amoral -- amoral miasma and amoral role by the United Nations that the Bosnian were understandably extremely skeptical, not to say, hostile, when you met with them to discuss these issues. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Finally, just on this subject, you've accepted, I think, that the Bosnian were outgunned, massively outgunned?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And that's due to two factors mainly, isn't it: That the Serb army -- first perhaps you can tell us as a military man, the JNA was what, the fourth largest army in Europe before the war?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Numerically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And it left all its hardware with the Bosnian Serbs when -- after May 19th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Bosnian Serb army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And secondly, the UN was maintaining an arms embargo on Bosnia which meant that the Bosnian couldn't get arms to defend themselves. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a third factor and that was that the Bosnian Serb army was being supplied, resupplied from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, still on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please make sure to make pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Apologies. I'll just take a few more pages before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. We have about eight minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Page 3483. It's just a passage at the bottom. This is a sitrep, is it, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And it is the 16th of March. "Town", could you read A.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A, tension largely dissipated. People, particularly refugees, still, however, in fear for their lives".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So that refers to the fact that after General Morillon said he would stay, some tension dissipated but people were still in fear for their lives?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you could turn to 3491, and that's the 17th of March. Just to clarify that it's correct, isn't it, that shells did actually start falling or were falling when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These shells that had fallen on the morning of the 17th of March, were the first shells to hit the town or near the town since we had arrived in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Do you know if those shells killed anyone?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that three people were killed and about ten were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, finally, before the break, 3493. This is the 17th of March. If we see 4 -- could you read 4, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I demand today humanitarian aid convoys by road or by helicopter. We cannot wait any longer". That commander has no cigarellos left.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it, actually, that General Morillon asked for brandy and Davidoff cigars to be specially dropped?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. That was said flippantly and General Jones, in fact, said that he had arranged for them to be put into the airdrop of radio batteries and microphone for the TACSAT that we had requested. Whether they ever were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That may be an appropriate moment for a break. I'll being moving on to a new area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before we proceed any further, Mr. Di Fazio, are there any developments on what your stuff -- were supposed to be pursuing this morning, or checking?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, there aren't. If Your Honours please. I've, during the break, continued to make enquiries, spoken to persons whom I hope will be able to expedite the final confirmation of this clearance and -- but I can't report anything positive to you at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, because when things go wrong, they go wrong. We have a problem, a technical problem, which we have encountered before, these last couple of weeks. I think we need technical assistance. The transcript scrolling is jammed. And we need -- Colonel, this will take around about two or three minutes, so there is no point in leaving the courtroom while it is fixed. In the meantime, I do enjoin you, as much as I can, to sort this out, because if Mr. Jones all of a sudden decides to change tactics and become difficult, I think we will have problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I appreciate the urgency of the situation, Your Honours, and I'm trying to get to the bottom of it as fast as I can. Whether we're going to have the matter resolved by the end of this session or not, I don't know, because there's a problem of time difference between those who may be able to assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These matters are usually exchanged non verbally, so I would imagine that there should be a record. I don't suppose that non verbals are thrown here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Anyway, I stress that it's a matter of grave importance to the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I said I would only be difficult from tomorrow. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Technicians are coming. So is Christmas. Sorry about this. It's something that I cannot help when it happens. Is there an idea what is causing this? Is it a fault in the system itself? Or what is it? I see. I see. I think what's going to happen now is what happened last time. Today's sittings will be recorded in -- now it seems that they are trying to save it all in one file. If this doesn't work, we will have a second file and then the two will be amalgamated later on. We'll let them do what needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just thinking to make some use of the time, I had the idea of the witness being provided with a copy of an exhibit which he can then look at during the next break. I can even pass it up to him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. That's a very good suggestion, Mr. Jones. I appreciate that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It occupies the witness, I think, if he wishes to be occupied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I thank you all for being patient with us. These things happen. There is very little we can do. We need to wait and I appreciate the quick intervention of our technicians to solve these problems that we get from time to time. I do appreciate that, because your quick intervention sometimes saves us a lot of time. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. For the record, I gave or I arranged for the witness to have a copy of the chapter from Larry Hollingsworth book "Merry Christmas, Mr. Larry". I would just ask, have you read that book?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't actually.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I will ask if possible during the next break, if you could have a read of it. Now, we were on page 3495 of the diary, or at least I'm moving on to that page. For the record, it would be the 17th of March?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And if you could just read 1a down to General.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heading of that section is "1200 hours, sitrep on airdrop. One, general", and general means nothing specific, not General as in the military rank. "A, pallets are retained by those who find them. They are willing to kill to keep what they find".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And you've explained that already. That's for the record though, that is, Muslims killing Muslims over food?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Bosniaks killing Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: When you spoke -- when you and General Morillon spoke to Naser Oric, he explained, didn't he, that raids were being carried out, not just for weapons ammunition, but also for food?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The things which he said it was ammunition, weapons, food and supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, I've handed you a copy of the chapter of Larry Hollingsworth book, partly because if you turn to the next page, 3496, there's a reference to his name there. And I'm going to ask you to read most of this page, although I may ask you to stop at various points. So if you could start with the paragraph at the top, Larry Hollingsworth.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Larry Hollingsworth describes the situation as the worst he has scene in the entire time -- in his entire time in the former Yugoslavia. Situation here unlike any other in Bosnia-Herzegovina".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If I could stop you there. I think there's also "in SR" after the situation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in Srebrenica, as the worst he has seen in his entire time in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about the limited efforts by the war committee to deal with the problem of distribution. Isn't it right, looking at the next paragraph, 2B, could you first read that, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Local authorities have sent soldiers to try and recover some supplies. As yet, no success".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And then the next sentence, please as well?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Local authorities do not have enough disciplined soldiers to secure any airdrop".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So it's right that you understood or you had intelligence to the effect that it was impossible to secure the sites, given the resources available to the authorities?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. By the "authorities", what I'm referring to here is the Srebrenica war committee.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And as far as you are concerned, they were the interlocutors on that matter, they were people to speak to on this issue?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the local people. The way that I describe is Hajrudin Avdic as the mayor of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
