utterances.text: Would it be right to say as far as matters concerning the town and matters of civilian law and order were concerned, you would go to Avdic and you would go to Oric for matters regarding military matters in the broader area. Would that be a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the general sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, following a bit further down, we have the assessment -- reference to the law of the jungle which you've spoken about. In fact, if we look at D, it looks like General Jones did send a parcel for the commander.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "D, have little hope of recovering our pallet dedicated to commander. Repeat law of the jungle rules". What actually happened is that the pallet for General Morillon was dropped by separate aircraft in a different location, the other side of Srebrenica. In other words, on the road between Srebrenica and Potocari which is the opposite direction from where the main airdrops were. We tried to go out to recover it. We heard it coming down and land about 300, 400 metres away. But by the time we got there, it had already been found by the refugees, Bosniaks, and had been ripped apart and there was nothing left. However, the next morning, the batteries and the microphone and the spare antenna and about 20 or 30 kilograms of food were handed in.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: While a displaced person perhaps enjoyed the brandy and cigars dedicated to the commander?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were in there, I hope he did enjoy them.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If you would turn to page 3497. It's 17th of March still.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And does it say "from Kiseljak 1300" in the middle there? Perhaps you could explain what that refers to.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "From Kiseljak 1300" is information that was provided to us from Kiseljak as opposed to information that I was providing from Srebrenica back to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And could you read 1 under that.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Is MMWG still in progress?" And "MMWG" is "mixed-military working group" which was the tripartite meetings that were being held in Sarajevo with Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Serbs and Bosniak Presidency, under the auspices of the United Nations in Sarajevo. These meetings took place at the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: It's really the next bit which I would be grateful if you could read out "refugee status"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Refugee sitrep from Larry Hollingsworth. Larry Hollingsworth had been spending a lot of time in the town and with the -- with members of the war committee, trying to help organise them because he had a lot of experience with these kind of situations". And Larry Hollingsworth gave a lengthy debrief to me which I passed back over the radio, over the next few pages. "The general situation, worse than any scene in Bosnia-Herzegovina, 18 houses burned, 100 destroyed, all houses damaged. Town elders, tired, lethargic, unable to make decisions, have little or no control. All information contradictory. All facts vague. Pre-war population of Srebrenica only 6.500. Population of opstina was 38.000. Population in Muslim pocket, 70.000. Population now in Srebrenica, plus/minus minus 20.000. I am told... "Population in 50 kilometre radius is now 80.000. I have no evidence of this. And they do not hold 50-kilometre radius of territory."

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If I can stop you there. This was from Larry Hollingsworth, this information?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was information he had gathered from speaking with people in the town, the war committee and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Was he generally a reliable source, in your dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was one of the most reliable people that was there and he was by far the best of the UNHCR people.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: We saw earlier in this diary, I won't mention the name of the person, but him giving you a description of a fellow employer as being perhaps prone to exaggeration. Would it be correct to say that Larry Hollingsworth was not prone to exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was utterly trustworthy, in our view.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Then if you could read -- you can skip the next paragraph and then at the bottom: "New arrival refugees", to the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "New arrival refugees had no food for five days or had few possessions. Are ragged and very dirty. Town people and longer term refugees clearly distinguishable. There are still some cars, horses and even small flock of sheep. There are two shacks selling meat; however, diet for most people is berries and yellow flour from hazelnut trees. This they grind down to meal from which a bright yellow loaf is made. Wood is plentiful. In the evening there are many fires. Water is mainly from river that looks contaminated".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I will stop you there. Thank you. One correction. I think you probably referred to cows and horses rather than cars.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. You are correct. It is cows, and horses.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: There was very little or no fuel for cars, was there, at this time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Then this information about this surrogate bread being made by grinding down flowers from trees, is that something you yourself saw?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was even given some of it to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: It's pretty unpalatable stuff, I would imagine?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like eating saw dust.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If you could carry on on the next page, 3499, from "the streets are filthy", please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Hospital dirty and overcrowded. Four doctors and one surgeon. All tired. Now enough drugs and medicines for -- less for antibiotics. Bed strength 100. Now 200 patients. A further 100 in a temporary ambulante. 24 war wounded. New arrivals at hospital this morning. Average death rate, 20 per day. Surprisingly, birth rate has increased. 300 born in hospital since 12 July 1992. Airdrop concept excellent. The planes are on time and accuracy remarkable. However, very little is gathered for the common good. Airdrop scene is unbelievable. Planes not visible. Shoots only heard as they crash to ground. Drops zone is crowded with starving people. Gun fights, knivings and fights are common. The distribution is to the fittest and strongest. The hospital claims four per night die at airdrop scene".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I will stop you there. Again this is from Larry Hollingsworth?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Did you understand that he had actually gone and witnessed with his own eyes the airdrop scene?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He actually went up on to the plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And you went to the hospital. Is what is said about the hospital there consistent with what you saw?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions are entirely consistent. The description of four doctors and one surgeon differs from my recollection. From my recollection there was actually only one doctor. There were three Medecins Sans Frontieres doctors and the rest were -- the rest were nurses, all nursing assistants or people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You wouldn't know, Colonel, who this one surgeon that there is reference to here, would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't. This is what Larry Hollingsworth told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Just on the airdrops. It was major Rex Dudley, wasn't it, who was coordinating the drops?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the American major and he had a sergeant chapel with him with a TACSAT radio set in order to coordinate the airdrops.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And was he an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Was he a source for a lot of your intelligence of the military situation in the area when you were there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say he was the source for about a third of it. About a third came from the UN military observers and about a third came from the War Presidency and a couple of occasions we met with Colonel Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, just again on this page, four lines from the bottom, there is no registration of refugees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So would the correct picture be people arriving the whole time, some of whom would be able-bodied men, possibly soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But starving.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And the authorities having no idea who was there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Sentence reads, "no registration of refugees nor any enthusiasm to feed and house new arrivals".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And then -- I will wait for the translation. Then the next page 3500, at the conclusion, again this is 17th of March, if you could just read the conclusion there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Conclusion: Situation bad. Need urgent convoy of 100 metric tons to feed desperate people, followed by second 100 metric ton convoy at earliest opportunity. Other convoys on weekly basis".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Whose conclusion was that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Larry Hollingsworth's conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I'm just going to skip forward a little bit now in time. If you go to page 3506, please. For the record, this would be the 18th of March, I believe. Just picking up on that reference about the need for a convoy, paragraph 4 there reads, does it not: "This convoy must come in", must in capitals, "people are dying".

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The context here is that UNHCR had -- are refused to allow convoy to go forward because they would not accept the conditions that the Serbs were placing upon the passage of the convoy, whether it had escorts or didn't have escorts or whether it dropped off some of its food in Bratunac to Serb refugees along the way. This particular convoy was a military convoy, in other words, under the command of General Morillon. And General Morillon was exasperated at that stage with what he perceived as being politicking by UNHCR for reasons he didn't particularly understand. And this was in addition to all the obstacles that the Serbs were putting in the way and he was getting angry and he said: "This convoy I command. I am ordering you move now. The situation is desperate".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Then turning the page to 3507. The Prosecution asked you some questions about this. I believe the military situation was read in a summary way. So just -- I just want to take these points briefly. It says there, "the Bosnian military situation is deteriorating even faster. Bosnian loosing around five villages a day. At current Serb rate of advance they would have taken the enclave -- entire pocket in two weeks' time". So, is it right, that's the sitrep which you sent to General Jones in Frankfurt on the 18th of March?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now looking at the refugee situation, which starts at the bottom, two refugee situation. We see, it's going to 3508: "Refugees still streaming into Srebrenica unabated". Is that the word?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: "UNHCR rep is succeeding in getting some refugees off the streets into damaged accommodation".

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is referring to Larry Hollingsworth and his efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And on that point, would you agree that the buildings in Srebrenica were largely without windows, due to the impact of bombing and shelling, shattering those windows?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- most windows were still in place. However, wherever there had been shells, then around that particular spot, there would be no -- no windows. So for example, the PTT building itself, when we were there, I think all the glass was in all the windows, but there were other houses and places in Srebrenica where there was no glass, for example, in the centre of town where I described that we found the cluster bomb casing and the evidence of -- there was no glass in any of those windows.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Were there repeated calls for plastic sheeting to be sent to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: What was that to be used for?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To cover over windows in order to keep heat in.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Just on this page again, it may have been dealt with, but meeting with Naser Oric last night, there's a reference to Bosnian military authorities being desperate, morale being rock bottom and then Oric stating that they would fight to the bitter end. You confirmed that was the contents -- or the gist of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the gist of the meeting the previous evening. By Bosnian military authorities, I was referring to Colonel Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now turning to the next page, 3509, the very top, a meeting with the president of the war committee and he is stating that Bosnians would be willing to hand in their weapons. Would it be right to say that you regarded Hajrudin Avdic, to whom that refers, as a player in your negotiations? He was someone who you considered had authority to discuss matters of this nature?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hajrudin Avdic was -- we considered Hajrudin Avdic to be an authority in Srebrenica and regarding civilian affairs and the organisation in the town. Because we had only been able to meet with Colonel Oric once, in other words, the previous evening, General Morillon had not -- not asked Hajrudin Avdic what he thought, as he was there and he engaged Hajrudin Avdic in conversation on a number of times. What did he think about things in the way that any responsible negotiator would engage the opinions of all those he's able to speak with.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You told us over the last couple of days that, as a general policy, you or General Morillon would want to deal with the people who could actually make things stick. Would it be fair to say that obviously that is your objective, it makes a lot of sense, but you didn't always speak to the person who necessarily was the person you needed to speak to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We spoke with the people who were able to -- able to speak with. By that stage, we had already detected a frostiness between the war committee and Colonel Oric, in as much as whenever we requested to speak with Colonel Oric or asked for messages to be passed they said, yes, they would try and pass them on. But they were -- they did not like Colonel Oric or did not -- there was some kind of distance and animosity that we didn't particularly understand. And so, therefore, it was clear, in our minds, that there were differences of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: When you in fact told -- and I may be skipping around a bit, but before your briefing in Sarajevo, there were different factions even within Srebrenica, different power groups?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was referring to the struggle that we believed that was taking place around that time between the Bosniak authorities in Tuzla and the Bosniak authorities in Sarajevo. The situation being that the authorities in Tuzla believed that the authorities in Sarajevo were willing to sacrifice other Bosniak issues in order to save their skins in Sarajevo and that they, the Bosniak authorities, in Tuzla, were much more effective against the Bosnian Serbs and much better fighters. What we, in Bosnia-Herzegovina command, were not clear of was Colonel Oric; Sarajevo's man or was he Tuzla's man? That's what we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. Well, going back to this relationship with the war committee, and I don't want to ask you to speculate because you told us you weren't sure what the frostiness was, but you have described morale as being rock bottom. Do you think Colonel Oric regarded perhaps the war committee as being defeatist in attitude? Could that be a source?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was very disparaging about the war committee and he did not -- it was clear from his meeting with us that he did not think much of them.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now just at the bottom of that page, again, there's a reference in the last two lines to the safe -- well, perhaps, it's best if you read the whole paragraph. "Commander's assessment. General Morillon considers..."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "General Morillon considers that opening of an air corridor for helicopters remains one of the major conditions to guarantee the safety of the population and to guarantee the safety of the evacuation of the wounded men".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. I will stop you there. Now, you were in Srebrenica on the 24th of March 1993, weren't you, for the evacuation by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were prevented from getting back into Srebrenica. We were actually outside -- in fact, we were at the Karakaj bridge between Bratunac and Srebrenica when I was trying to communicate on the HF radio to Srebrenica and suddenly the -- my radio transmissions were jammed and as I was remarking to General Morillon, they're jamming us, I saw the first helicopters fly -- not overhead, but I saw them flying towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Serbs on that day shelled the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. The Serbs shelled the helicopter landing site. They killed and injured a number of soldiers amongst whom were two of the Canadian soldiers of the armoured personnel carrier that was with us. I went and examined, later, the shell craters in the HRS and interviewed a number of people about the shell fire. And what happened is that early in the morning, the Serbs did what is called registering a target. It's where you fire with one gun a couple of shells until that gun targets -- shells are landing on target. Then you stop. And the correction that you apply to that one gun you then apply to other guns, so that then every gun is pointing in parallel to be able to fire at the same location. Later in the day, when the helicopters came in, then the Serbs started shelling the landing site and caused a number of deaths and injuries. When I was -- so that meant that the Serbs had to have somebody who was watching, could physically see the helicopter landing site.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: A forward controller?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A forward controller.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And they walk it in right into the target?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Except they had already done that with what the exercise I call the registration of the target at the beginning of the day, so that they could later open fire, knowing, that unless the weather had changed and the wind had changed direction, that the shells would land in the right spot. I later, when General Morillon and I left Srebrenica and we were driving down the road from Zvornik to Pale, we came across an obstacle where a jackknifed lorry had blocked the road for about six hours and we used the armoured personnel carrier to drag this truck out of the way. There is a long cue of traffic there and waiting there was a staff car with a Serb Colonel and a Serb -- Bosnian Serb special forces officer who started talking with me about having been on training courses with the -- with the SES and he described to me events which had happened at the PTT building in a way that I was absolutely certain that that man had been watching what had happened. He then described that he knew how to direct artillery fire and I believe it was that man who directed that artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And so for our purposes, we have General Morillon basically signalling that for the enclave safety to be assured -- the enclave safety, but for the population to be reassured, evacuation of the wounded by helicopter was a necessary gesture or condition.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The context was that the Serbs were threatening that they would allow women and children to be evacuated but not the men, because they claimed that they were war crimes in amongst the men. So therefore we needed the helicopters to evacuate the men so that they would be passed -- so they would not pass through Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And by shelling the evacuation, the Serbs were signalling that they would have none of that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, if I could pass up the next exhibit to everyone else which is a chapter on Srebrenica from "Merry Christmas Mr. Larry", because I have a question in that regard. Sorry with the usher's assistance, please. In the meantime for the Colonel, I can indicate it's page 207, and it's paragraph 4. I will just read it. "General Morillon was not having the success he wanted in arranging helicopter evacuation. The Serbs were not happy. They suspected that "war criminals" would be included in the evacuation. Their definition of war criminal seemed to be any male between the age of 16 and 60". In fact, that reflects very much just what you've told us?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that the Serbs were not letting out any -- were not prepared to let out any men on the pretext that they were war criminals?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What the Serbs were telling us was that there were war criminals amongst the men, that they had lists of who these war criminals -- these alleged war criminals were and that they wished to establish the identity of every single man who was evacuated from Srebrenica in order to establish whether any of them were war criminals before letting them pass. They did not say to us that any Bosniak male is a war criminal. In other words, as per here. What they said is they had a list of war criminals with which to check -- anybody who was evacuated against that list.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And that's what they said in July 1995 as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. Moving on to page 3514, that's the 18th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you move to page 35 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I need an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will give this exhibit number D218.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D218. Colonel, while we are with this -- you still have this document, photocopies from this book still in your hands. Can I direct you to -- there are some photos starting on page 211. If you skip a couple and you arrive at the photo where you have top right -- top left, an historic General Morillon behind the window with the megaphone. It says, "A historic moment, General Morillon declaring Srebrenica under the protection of the United Nations. Courtesy of Tony Birtley". Then just below that, there is: "Me with Dr. Nadret Mukanovic, the legendry surgeon of Srebrenica after the war in the safety of Tuzla hospital". Do you have an explanation why Larry Hollingsworth would describe Dr. Nadret Mukanovic as the legendary surgeon of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no explanation. It was not our experience and observation that Dr. Mukanovic had anything to do with the Srebrenica hospital at the time that we were there. What happened subsequently, I obviously cannot comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I could take you to page 207, please which is the same page where you were referred to -- which you were referred to earlier on by Mr. Jones. You have penultimate paragraph: "I organised a meeting with the authorities and with Nadret from the hospital. Based on Simon Mardell's list, it shows 97 patients. We received ten trucks, that would be roughly ten patients per truck. The journey from Srebrenica to Tuzla would take up to 8 hours. It would be a bumpy, miserable ride but ten to a truck would give them room to breathe". Does that give you the impression, at least, that the author of this book projects or depicts Nadret Mukanovic as someone who had the major say when it came to the hospital in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. What it describes to me is that he was making decisions outside the hospital, not actually inside the hospital. As a member of the -- of the war committee.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If I may pursue that a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If you could turn to page 192. Very top: "We entered the hospital, turned left and climbed the stairs. At the top of the first flight, there were patients on beds in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. 192.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: "We entered the hospital", et cetera. "We were met by the surgeon, Dr. Nadret Mukanovic who was a captain in the army". A bit further down. "By this time he was an experienced war surgeon but a troubled man with deep dark rings around his eyes, a man who moved in wild jerky bursts. He spoke with great warmth and admiration about Simon Mardell". Concluding with, "I have his patient assessment list here". Then you will see for the next page there is what is described on page 193 as a "desperate litany of the needs of the hospital" which Dr. Mukanovic told the internationals. In fact, it's a subject I am coming to but I suggest to you that, Dr. Mukanovic was not a loiterer outside the hospital who was not a real doctor but was very much a heroic figure in the war hospital. Do you accept you might have misjudged him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I told you is what I saw. I was not present at these meetings, so I cannot comment on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Jones, you can refer the witness also to what there is on page 208.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Where Nadret is in the operating theatre? Is that the section which Your Honour has in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It continues, "I found him operating on a patient". It says, "Larry, good, please have you a torch? Can you shine it in here? He's asked pointing to the open stomach of the patient he was assisted by another doctor", et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. Do you have any reason why you would doubt --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt it if this is what Larry said he saw, then that's what Larry said he saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I won't belabour this point further, Mr. Jones, or should we leave it at that and move to something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can leave it -- there was on this subject one more subject I wanted to put. I'm slightly skipping ahead. But some war hospital, which I believe is Exhibit D119 - there is no need for us all to have in front of us - but it's a chapter called Nadret, about Dr. Mukanovic. It says on Page 75, "But he wore tinted eyeglasses in part to protect his blepharitic eyes from painful light."

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So I did want to suggest to you that the fact that Dr. Mukanovic was wearing sunglasses was not an affectation as you might have suggested, that he had a medical condition requiring him to wear sunglasses?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I will leave the subject now. Can I ask you please to turn to page 3514 of the diary. This is the 18th of March. And a sitrep. I take it again this is intelligence from the UNMOs, that the "rate of incoming artillery fire has increased substantially since last visit"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a report made by the UNMOs to me.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Can you read the next sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "UNMOs came under direct shell fire twice. Having to leave vehicle and take cover with rounds of artillery fire that is landing within 100 metres of them".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I actually wanted you to read the last sentence of the previous paragraph, which refers to counting 80 rounds per hour.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Rate of incoming artillery fire had increased substantially since last visit. UNMOs counted 40 rounds per hour in immediate vicinity".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's in the immediate vicinity of Osmace and the grid references we have at 1, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Then it's also stated at C that UNMOs collected cluster bomb ...

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dispensers.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Dispensers?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly at Osmace. Cluster bomb dispensers are actually the empty cases.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So Osmace was coming under severe attack in this whole period, would that be the intelligence you had?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to check elsewhere in the diary, but certainly at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If you could turn to the next page, 3515. 18th March. It's 2c, which I am interested in. "Craters along the main refugee withdrawal routes would indicate that claims by refugees are being shelled whilst fleeing were true." So is that the intelligence as well?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was provided by the UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And as a person who has spent time in Bosnia and as a military man, would you think of any reason why you would shell people who were already fleeing?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to terrorise them further.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving forward to the 21st of March -- sorry, first, page 3520. This is just to clarify an aspect of the negotiations which you had. It's one, near the top: "No Serbs in Tuzla who wish to leave. Any who wish to leave did so beginning of war".

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At beginning -- at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, is it right -- is my understanding correct that a constant refrain from the Serbs was that the Serbs in Tuzla should leave, should be allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should be allowed to leave and it was their belief or their allegation that the Bosniak Presidency forces and authorities were preventing them from leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any credible evidence this that was the case? Or intelligence?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were in Tuzla, we met with UNHCR people -- we also met with Tuzla authorities and we asked them about this and their opinion was that the majority had -- who had wanted to leave had already left and that of the remainder, the majority wanted to stay, but there was a small number who actually did genuinely want to leave but were afraid to say so. And that seemed a reasonable representation. We had no reason to disbelieve that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that this was an example of what I think was referred to as linkage, where the sides would try to link an issue with an issue of their own so that --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere else, yes. It was a constant bedevilment of all negotiations in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: What were the Serbs linking this issue with Tuzla Serbs to, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were linking the release of Tuzla Serbs with the evacuation of people from Srebrenica and with the delivery of humanitarian aid into Srebrenica. In other words, they were saying they would not allow either of those two latter to happen until the Serbs civilians in Tuzla were allowed to leave Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Did you fear that that sort of blackmail in essence could lead you to be participating in ethnic cleansing, in the sense that you would be -- you were under pressure to make Serbs leave Tuzla in order to be able to feed starving people in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not in any way involved with making Serbs leave Tuzla. As far as we were concerned, if any Serbs wished to leave Tuzla, and requested to do so, then we would help them. But we were not going to do so at anybody's request. Regarding your second question, which was: Was that effectively aiding and abetting ethnic cleansing? What was it, saving lives or ethnic cleansing? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: We may come to some of those philosophical issues and we may not. For the time being, I just want to refer you to 3521 in the diary. This is the 20th of March, I think you will agree. You will see there is a 3 --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's the 20th of March, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And paragraph 4 or point 4 which I will tried to read. "For BHC Kiseljak, Bosnia-Herzegovina command, Kiseljak only ..."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: "Command."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Commander trying to get some Serbs held by Bosnians in Srebrenica released tomorrow."

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, this was on the 20th of March, correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: This appears to have been an initiative of General Morillon to release any Serbs held in Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Serbs held in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: It says SR, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. You are absolutely correct. This is -- this is nothing to do with the -- I was confused by the previous subject that we were talking about. No. This is talking about prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: There may be a problem with interpretation. I'm informed that my client is not receiving or any -- any of the Bosnian speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a problem indeed. I have to address your client through you, Mr. Jones. Could you please ask him what was the last interpretation that he received?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. It was my last question and we have interpretation now, so I think I can probably resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We can solve it very easily. First, I want to make sure he is receiving interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could you please repeat your last question, Mr. Jones, and you, Colonel, please, try to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I will put it this way. Does this state, on page 3521, point 4: "For BHC Kiseljak only. Commander trying to get some Serbs held by Bosnian in SR released tomorrow"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now is it right this was an initiative, in a sense, of General Morillon already on the 20th, that he was trying to achieve this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Morillon had been asking and had mentioned to Colonel Oric on the 17th that he wished to -- he was suggesting to Colonel Oric, it was pointless holding prisoners. If you have any, give them up. Please give them over, at least to help create some small amount of goodwill.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: But Colonel Oric never acknowledged or never gave any indication that he was holding anyone on the 17th of March?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So is General Morillon guessing that there might be prisoners, or he was basing himself on information which he had received from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From -- and I can't remember whether it was Major Dudley or from Mihailov, one of them had said that they had, in speaking with or hearing from people in the town, that there were some prisoners held somewhere in the town, so therefore General Morillon believed that there were prisoners but didn't know where.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. So either from Major Dudley or from Mihailov. And so when we turn to the 21st of March, which I am coming to, as far as the appearance of a prisoner who was then being returned to the other side, this was not some spontaneous occurrence out of the blue. This was a follow up, an initiative by General Morillon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Morillon had asked -- suggested to Colonel Oric that it would be good to hand over or release any prisoners, if he had any. Having heard from Major Dudley or Mihailov that people in the town said they were prisoners, General Morillon had also, obviously, asked the -- the War Committee, president of the War Committee, "Are there prisoners in the town?" And the response was, "I don't know. It's not my -- it's not my authority. It's not my issue." General Morillon said, "Well, if you do know of where they are," then, again, he suggested they should be released. "Why don't you do so?" And -- or asked that they are released. When, on the next --

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm coming to that. Thank you. So in other words, the identical request which General Morillon made about releasing prisoners was made to Colonel Oric and to the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But with neither admitting or recognizing that -- that they held prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, speaking of the meeting on the 18th of March, you described how Oric appeared --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: The 17th. My apologies. That he appeared downcast, but that he was almost confiding in General Morillon. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Did you always find in your dealings with Colonel Oric that he was candid with you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And on the 17th of March, in that meeting, as far as you could tell, was he speaking with complete frankness on all the subjects that were discussed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our impression. It was as if he could speak with General Morillon about these issues, but there was nobody else that he could speak with about them and certainly not with the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: At that meeting he was talking about some pretty desperate things, fighting to the last man, that sort of thing. He wasn't holding anything back, was he?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in -- not in our opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So did it strike you, when he didn't acknowledge or didn't respond to the request about prisoners, that he wasn't being evasive but perhaps he simply didn't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not draw any conclusion. We didn't know. He had far more dangerous and worrisome issues on his mind than -- I do not wish to sound callous, but than -- than prisoners. There was much, much more on his mind than prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, turning to the events of the 21st of March. You described -- you described what you saw, a person who resembled, as you put it, a victim of the concentration camps practically. I take it, then, that was a dramatic memorable experience?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, we established your entries in the diary for the 21st of March starting on 3524. Now, there you refer to something occurring at 0800, I couldn't fully decipher it.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is "21 March, 0800, HF from BH Command Kiseljak"; in other words, an incoming message.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And then on the next page, 3525, "Meeting in Bratunac"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: At what time on the 21st of March did this release occur?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been about 9.30, something -- it was in the morning. It was literally just before we went to Bratunac. In fact, that was why I was down by the vehicles, getting ready to depart to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, firstly, that you didn't make a contemporaneous note and it's not a --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. The only reference to the event is actually when I reported it the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And that's on 34 -- my apologies. One moment. Yes. Sorry. 3536. If there is "we released a wounded Serb prisoner. We know of two more Serbs held by Bosnian forces in SR whose command is trying to get released."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: That's the only mention in the diary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You dealt with the post-it note earlier which you put in many years later. Was that post-it after you had been contacted by the Prosecution in relation to this case, that that was added?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't remember. What I do remember is that this prisoner release was something that was very vivid in my memory. And I didn't touch any of my diaries for Bosnia for about five or six years after the event. And then I started looking back again. And I was searching where on earth was the reference to the prisoner. And I was looking through it and that's why it was, if you remember you made the comment yesterday, it was inserted in between because I then found, oh, that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you given evidence in any other trial here in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Ganic -- sorry. Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, this message was sent by TACSAT, is that correct, 3536?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it was. It says at the top of the page, "21 March, 2100 by TACSAT to Kiseljak".

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So does that mean in Kiseljak there would be a printed message with this text included?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would expect there to be.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, I need to go through this instant with you in some detail. First of all, let's start with the PTT building. If you could tell us, firstly, which internationals were there when this car arrived as you described it.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Canadian crew of the APC, Mihailov, I believe General Morillon was actually still inside the building. Those are the only ones that I can explicitly recall.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: For the Canadian crew, are you able to recall the names of those members of the crew?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you who the five members of the crew were. It was not all five who accompanied us. It was usually only two or three who accompanied us. And -- did you want me to give you the names?

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes. I believe they're in your diary.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are. It was Sergeant Morrison, he was the commander, Master Corporal Paris, Private Charron, Private Parrell, and Private McAllister.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: All right. So it was two or three of that crew, but you don't know which of them it was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember which. It was probably not Sergeant Morrison, but it probably was Colonel Paris and Private McAllister, because they were usually the person who commanded the vehicle and McAllister was the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And they were there when as you described it this Mercedes pulled up, did a hand-brake turn, they would have seen what you saw?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they had their heads up at that time or whether they were inside the vehicle at that moment, I can't recall. But they were around the vehicle. They were with us when we went up to follow the Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: As far as the arrival of the Mercedes is concerned, I'm not going to belabour it because our client isn't charged with reckless driving, but I wonder if you would agree any car driving in Srebrenica would be a prime target for shelling by the Serbs, as indicative that an important person was inside.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, though no such shelling was taking place of that kind at that time. There was no sniping going on at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Srebrenica was surrounded by hills, correct, and the Serbs occupied the high points?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. The hills surrounding Srebrenica there were not in the hands of the Serbs. That was the point I was making earlier about the forward observation officer, who was -- he was in those hills at an earlier occasion, and must have been able to see in. But the Serbs did not hold the high ground.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Just to clarify that. The helicopter evacuation, on the 24th of March, was very much in the town of Srebrenica, wasn't it? It was a football pitch which was in the environ, if I can put it that way, of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica is a long thin town. And the football pitch is at the very end of the town, closest to Potocari. In fact, from the football field, you could not even see the PTT building, never mind the rest of the town. There was a bend in the valley.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now going back to the 21st of March, and I'm going to suggest to you and I don't want you to answer at this stage, but that you are mistaken about saying that it was Oric who you saw coming out of the car and whom you saw subsequently. So I am going to be referring to the person whom you claim was Oric, rather than Oric. Firstly, throughout this whole episode, do you say that the person you saw was able to move about in a fully functioning way, had no problems walking or generally getting around?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was swaggering. Sorry. No. He was not -- he was entirely fit and healthy and he was, in fact, so fit and healthy that he was swaggering.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance I would like to pass up two exhibits which are medical certificates. I will start with the first one and deal with them separately, dated 18th of January, 2000. Sorry, if you would give me a moment, Your Honours. You will see, this is a certificate to the effect that Naser Oric was in fact wounded on the 15th of March, 1993 in Pricevac by pieces of a tank grenade and I will further suggest that in fact it was damage to his Achilles tendon which he suffered. Now, do you say the person you saw was not limping or on crutches or being supported by other people?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Neither had the -- Colonel Oric -- or the person who we met in Konjevic Polje been limping in any way, nor had the person who we met on the 17th been limping or moving in any way that indicated he was incumbered.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Well dealing with Konjevic Polje firstly, that was before the 15th of March, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the fifth and 6th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1993, yes. Sorry sir.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And as far as the meeting on the 17th was concerned, I think I'm correct in saying -- but correct me if I'm wrong -- you described how Oric was there one minute and not there the next. Did you actually see him arrive?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: He was seated when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was getting up and walking around and sitting down and he was very troubled. And I saw him leave that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And I will also pass up another exhibit which is on the same theme as the first one but dated the 2nd of August, 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this first one I take it you are tendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be D519.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the next one will be D520.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That seems rather high numbers for our exhibits. I thought we were up to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. It is D219 -- 219 and 220. Not 519. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In fact, if I may, I don't have questions about the second document. I would be putting the same point to the witness, which hardly seems worth it. I would ask for -- well you have given it an exhibit number, so I can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, on this thing, it's correct isn't it that in your diary you didn't mention seeing Oric specifically on that day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the diary. The record is as we've already described.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, you then described how you went to another location following the Mercedes. Who, among the internationals, if I can put it that way, went to the second location?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the crew of the Canadian armoured personnel carrier, Mihailov, General Morillon and myself. As I say there may have been others, but I can't remember. Those are -- the ones I've just told you are the ones I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You were in the APC, were you, with the others?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: But you don't remember who else was there, apart from the Canadians, Morillon and Mihailov?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You do maintain that you have a clear recollection of this event?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All too clear.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Were any UNMOs present either at the PTT building or at the second location?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may well have been.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: But you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: How about the Americans, Chapple and Dudley?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm pretty sure they were not there. But there may have been -- may have been UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. You're pretty sure that Chapple and Dudley were not there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, in terms of any conversations which took place that day between the person who you say is Oric and Morillon, you weren't actually present for those conversations, were you? You weren't within earshot?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was within ear shot for a brief period at the very beginning. The conversations were between this person and Mihailov.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now was that at the PTT building or at the second location?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was outside the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. So for that conversation, you don't know what was said?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because it was in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And then the second location, I think it was, you described -- well perhaps it wasn't even at the second location, but a conversation which General Morillon related to you which he had had with the person you say was Oric. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And you weren't present for that conversation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And that conversation would have been conducted in what language?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been conducted in Serbo-Croat between this person and Mihailov with Morillon present.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Did Mihailov speak French?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Fluently. He was a French foreign legion soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So barracks, French perhaps. Did you see this man, the prisoner placed on a stretcher at any point?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall who the stretcher bearers were?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Canadians. It was a Canadian stretcher that was taken out of the armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And this person, this prisoner was removed from a private house as you described it by Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From behind the private house. He was brought along the side of the house. In other words not out through a door. So where he came from, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And he was being held by Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Who then outside handed him over to blue helmets?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Between this building and the armoured personnel carrier which is in the middle of the road, so sort of where the pavement would have been if there had been a pavement.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And during this process, the person you say was Oric was present, but not one of the people actually --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I was going to say, actually holding the prisoner?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can -- sorry to butt in at this stage. If I were to show you a street diagram of the PTT and its environs, would you be able to indicate to us more or less where this house was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More or less. I could not -- if you were to show me photographs of houses, I would be able to say not that one, not that one. It could look like that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution have a street diagram of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Not that I can think of as I stand here. I know there is an overhead photograph that we've got of Srebrenica that may be of some use. In fact it may even be in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But I don't recall anything that is more detailed off the top of my head. I can certainly find out and cause enquiries to be made today, soon, now. And I will try and get whatever information we can provide to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps in re-examination. I wasn't planning to show the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would imagine so. But what other public buildings in Srebrenica do you recollect, apart from the PTT and the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recollect any other public buildings, official buildings. I recollect private houses. I recollect blocks of flats and I recollect shops and a -- I recollect a department store.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at the second location when the prisoner was handed over to the Canadians, were you on the street or standing around, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was stand -- we had all -- we weren't sure what to expect. We stopped the vehicle. And when the two Bosniaks with the -- this prisoner between them came round the side, round the side of the house, we then realized what it was. We loaded the ramp of the armoured personnel carrier, and we all got out and I got out and stood there. The two Canadians got the stretcher out. The two Bosniaks helped lay the -- the Canadians lay the man on the stretcher.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And did you recognise either of these two Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was ... In dark winter camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You can't say anything of what their affiliation would be?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the war committee present?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So you only recognised internationals or you only remember recognizing the Canadians as being at the second location. You can't mention any other names of people who might have seen this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There might have been other people who happened to be passing in the street, but this was, it was actually completely unexpected and we drove there, stopped and -- but that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, on this occasion, you had seen -- you had met Oric twice, I think, is that correct? Once in Konjevic Polje and once on the 17th of March?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Each meeting had been relatively brief?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- in Konjevic Polje it had been a couple of hours the first night. About half an hour in the morning. And then probably about three quarters of an hour around lunch time. On the evening of the 17th it had been probably a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And you saw him seated most of the time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that -- during that time, but he had -- as I said, he had arrived at Konjevic Polje. It would be wrong to say that I only saw him seated, but, yes, it would be correct to say that most of the time that I was in his presence he was seated.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now I would suggest to you, in fact, at this time in Srebrenica there's quite a few able-bodied men with beards. There is nothing particularly distinctive about Naser Oric's appearance. I would suggest to you that you could be mistaken when you say that it was Oric who you saw on that day.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed -- correct or incorrectly -- that I was seeing Oric, but more significantly to me, it was Mihailov who had the conversations with him. And it was -- and Mihailov had said, Oric said this, Oric said that, et cetera. So it never occurred to me that this might be anyone else, and to be honest, as I'm here, I did not personally carry out the conversations with Colonel Oric, because obviously I didn't speak Serbo-Croat, but Mihailov did. And I would find it surprising if Mihailov, in speaking with somebody, would realise that he was speaking with somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So your statement that it was Oric is based not so much on any physical identification or recognition, but on what Mihailov said? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's not what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Quite -- it's too clear -- two clear basis for his reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken, Mr. Di Fazio, but, please, let the witness answer the question. I think he is intelligent enough to know what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, but I think I am able to clarify a matter of this importance.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Given what you have just said about Mihailov, is it right that your belief that it was Oric is based largely on what Mihailov told you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is based on my seeing what I believe I saw, which was reinforced by what Mihailov said.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Finally, do you know where Mihailov is today, if he is living or what his current whereabouts are?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My belief is that he is -- that he retired from the French army, but you would need to speak with General Morillon to -- I'm sure Morillon knows where he is.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Will you give me one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, while Mr. Jones confers, there is a matter that I would like to raise with you before we adjourn for this particular session, that could be done in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We've got one, two minutes before the break -- before we get to the break in any case, Mr. Jones. Shall we stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please escort the witness. We will reconvene in about half an hour's time, Colonel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can we just briefly go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So from what I gather, having heard you, Mr. Di Fazio, and you Mr. Jones, I think we need a good 30-minute break, during which you will carry out what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you will update us immediately as soon as we resume. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, can you update the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. The issue I raised with you in private session has been resolved satisfactorily, copies of the diary have been made available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously in terms of the plan, we haven't had a chance to look at the diary, but tomorrow I plan to deal with anything arising from that, and then the other documents, if we can resolve that. So I will try to just finish the diary today and maybe some other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Going back now to the diary on the 21st of March, 1993. Do you have 3525 open, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So did you, in fact, once this prisoner had been put in the APC, did you then all travel to Bratunac and then you had this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And it appears to be a meeting with General Morillon, yourself, Mihailov. Denuyft was an UNMO, wasn't he, from Belgium?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the names right here are Morillon, Denuyft, who is a Belgian major, Commandant Beary. Commandant is major in the Irish army. It's quite possible that those, when I said earlier, that there may have been UNMOs present, logically, it would suggest that if there were UNMOs present, it would be those.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Present at the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the PTT building. And for their present -- at the PTT building, at the initial arrival, I can't comment, but they would much more likely be present at the handover of the prisoner, because we departed straight from there to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for clarification, did both the UNMOs and the Canadians wear blue helmets?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Canadians certainly wore blue helmets. I wore blue helmet. Mihailov wore blue helmets. The UNMOs usually wore a blue beret, not helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. And then on the Serb side, did you actually meet with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We had been told that Mladic would be there. We actually met with General Gvero and the president of the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Would that be Milan Gvero?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General -- yes, I think it is it Milan Gvero. We met him many times over the previous number of months.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: You may or may not be able to help us with that but is that the same Milan Gvero who has been indicted by this Tribunal for crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I assume that there is no dispute that Mladic is the same Mladic is the same Mladic who is indicted for genocide in relation to Srebrenica to the events in July of 1995. Among others.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope he burns in hell.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. The next page, 3526, there is a comment lines 19 to 21, 21 isn't there. It is Morillon speaking. And he says: "My intention to demilitarise Srebrenica, Muslims hand weapons to UNPROFOR, only allow police with side arms".

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: That's confirming what you said earlier, that civilian police with side arms and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not soldiers and not military police.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to 3528, it's the same meeting. And is it correct that Morillon says: "You have already won. I'm trying to help you, too, for you to capture Srebrenica" --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 3528.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to help you underlined, too, you to capture Srebrenica would be diplomatic disaster?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And crime against humanity. If you just stop now would be very good for your image?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Do you know why General Morillon considered that it would be a crime against humanity for the Serbs to take Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment specifically, but in general, because doing so would cause many casualties amongst the large number of refugees and civilians who were concentrated in the pocket and who were under -- in the terrible kind of conditions we have discussed over the last couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Would it be fair to summarise that on the 21st of March, 1993, that basically everyone knew at that stage that if Srebrenica fell to the Serbs, there would be massacres?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- that was our belief, that there would be very many casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, I think you went to a funeral Kravica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The funeral itself was at a church in Bratunac, on the outskirts of Bratunac. We then went after that to the Kravica location.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, are you aware that Kravica was the centre of Serb nationalism going back at that to the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Were you aware of its tactical significance?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tactical significance is that it was a town which was on the road between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac, and if that road was held by the Bosniaks, then for Serbs to go from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje, Konjevici, which by that stage they had captured, they would have had to go all the way around via Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, you had many conversations with the Serbs about the attack or action on Kravica on Orthodox Christmas, 1993. Wasn't that one of the complaints that had occurred on Orthodox Christmas, that that was considered particularly atrocious?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accusation was A, that the people had been killed. Secondly, was that it had been deliberately done on the Orthodox Christmas in order to -- Balkan diplomacy.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were actually in Sarajevo, weren't you, on that day, Orthodox Christmas 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I've looked at pages 15 and 16 of your 2002 statement for Galic. I'm not going to put that in front of you. I just refer to it. The ERN number for the record is 02192822 and 02192823. Under the heading Bosnian Serb year end celebrations, it says: "On Christmas Eve, exactly at midnight, every Bosnian Serb heavy weapon around Sarajevo started firing and continued firing into the city for about 20 minutes. It did the same again on the Serb Greek-Orthodox Christmas Eve, 7 January." And then on page 16, the next page: "It was like a fireworks display, except lethal. For example I watched a rapid-fire 40-millimetre Bofors gun sited above the residency, hammering out a tune "x x xxxx x x" for twenty minutes", the Xs to signify that tune for 20 minutes, "firing hundreds of rounds into the city." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was horrific.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, the Serbs did wage war on their holiday, their Orthodox Christmas, killing people?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So it's fair to say they didn't treat it as a day of peace and goodwill to mankind?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no days of peace and goodwill at that unfortunate time.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And just for the diary a bit longer. I'm skipping forward, if you will give me a moment. 3546. This would be on the 21st of March.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: I know it's rather difficult to read, but 6c.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 6c reads: "Commander intends leaving Srebrenica Wednesday 24 March with medivac, if UNMOs have been deployed." That was referring to planned helicopter evacuation that we mentioned previously.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: An then if we look at B. Sorry about taking it in reverse order. Can you read that, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Commander awaits success of evacuation of Serbs from Tuzla before continuing to try and get UNMOs in."

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So is it right that General Morillon accepted that linkage to a certain extent, that UNMOs coming to Srebrenica was conditioned on Serbs leaving Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The linkage that he was tacitly accepting was people from Tuzla, Serbs from Tuzla leaving Tuzla and people from Srebrenica leaving Srebrenica.
