General Morillon had, by that stage, insisted with the Serbs that there could be no linkage regarding getting UNMOs in or out. UNMOs coming in was something which the Serbs had to accept. And initially they did not, that is back on the 17th and 18th. But by that stage, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page, 3547, we see number five there. Doesn't that read: "Commander wishes to be informed by HF radio the moment the convoy with Serbs leaves Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters please ask the witness to read the diary a bit more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Five: Commander wishes to be informed by HF radio," that's high-frequency radio, "the moment the convoy with Serbs leaves Tuzla. He will then immediately go to Bratunac to get the UNMOs in. UNMO should stand by and be ready to move as soon as the convoy leaves Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: So in the end, wasn't it a classic absolute trade-off, that even down to the moment Serbs left Tuzla, only then could UNMOs go in.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly coincidental timewise.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: What I'm driving at is basically this: Didn't the Serbs in fact call the shots pretty much for what was going on in the enclave, including deployment of UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sadly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And just moving to the last few entries. 3550. This would be the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 23 March, 12.40 Zvornik Karakaj bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm on 3550. Perhaps I've -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 3550. He's read the line halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. I'm actually referring to the very first two lines. Is it right that you met the imam of Srebrenica and that he reported that 40 villages in the south-east were under threat?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now we move forward to 3555. This is the 24th of March. Just if you could clarify. These notes record, do they not, the Serbs shelling the evacuation of the wounded from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, 3556. And looking to the second-to-last paragraph at the bottom, could you read that and explain what that is about.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Regional government utterly disprove of General Morillon's approach which leads to ethnic cleansing." And that is reference to the point of view stated by the Tuzla authorities, from -- we met them in Tuzla and why they did not wish to allow the Serb -- the Serbs in Tuzla to leave Tuzla and why they did not wish people, refugees in Srebrenica to leave Srebrenica. Their point of view was that that was tantamount to ethnic cleansing and the supporting and the facilitation of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Wasn't that a view also expressed by Oric to you and General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recollect that coming up in discussion in that manner between Colonel Oric and General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And then moving forward to just the last few final entries. At 3559. This would be the 24th of March. This is a meeting with President Milosevic in Belgrade. Would that be right, minutes of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: See on 3559, the second paragraph, can you read what that says.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "World focussed on Srebrenica. Your friends in Bosnia are mad enough to continue the offensive. Bosnians only have small arms and" --

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Okay, we can stop there. We've touched already on the complete disequilibrium in terms of weaponry between Serbs and Muslims. Which that refers to, I take it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And it also refers to the Bosnian Serbs. That is, as opposed to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: In fact I think you told us just even a small rocket launch in Srebrenica was like gold dust?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Now, if we can move forward to 3565. This would be the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3565 is the 26th of March. The meeting in Belgrade with Mladic and Gvero and a number of others.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And so on 3565, starting from line 18, could you just read out what General Morillon said and what that was about.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This madman betrayed promise. You gave your personal guarantee for airlift. This madman, who has obviously lost his nerve, fired at UN helicopters and location of evacuation of heavily wounded. Luckily results were limited at two wounded soldiers and three civilians killed."

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Then just further down, about six lines from the bottom: "We'll give you proof of madness." If you can carry on from there.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We'll give you proof of madness when shelled UN soldiers at stadium -- when crowd waiting and on helicopters in Srebrenica. Initiative of this brute could have disastrous consequences on world reaction."

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, General Gvero, what did you understand his position was at this time in the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our understanding was that Gvero was like the second in command, but that he was not particularly effective. Mladic called all the shots. Tolimir was the vicious Rottweiler, the political commissar. Gvero was the lap-dog who was trotted out.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And when you speak about negotiating or facilitating cease-fires in Srebrenica between the Muslims and the Serbs, isn't it right the Bosniaks were having to deal on the other side with people like Gvero, having to put their people in trust in people like Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, there's been no evidence of any negotiations that this witness has touched upon between Bosniaks and the -- and the Serbs. This witness has only given evidence of his facilitating and his acting, so it's not -- a point not without significance. I have not heard of any direct negotiations between the Bosniaks and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did. I did. Earlier on in his testimony he did mention that tripartite or tripartite meetings that were going on between the Presidency, Sarajevo, the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I know. I recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's the only thing I recall. Of course I stand could be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I could rephrase that. I didn't mean to suggest there were direct contacts. I can rephrase the question, if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think if you do that perhaps we will surpass this impasse or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Yes. During this period, Colonel, you and General Morillon were going back and forth between the parties, weren't you, trying to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: And on the Serb side, the people who you were trying to make deals with, which you would then present to the Bosniaks, were Gvero, Mladic, Karadzic, those people?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We believed that it was only when we spoke with Mladic that things would happen. We believed that Gvero was put in front of us in order to obstruct and to delay.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Did the Bosniaks ever say to you: We can't trust these people, these Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Sir, if you will bear with me for a moment. Yes. I'm finished with the direct, except for one thing. If you could just help us with page 3601, which in the original is probably right towards the back. And it's just really seeking clarification or confirmation that the list of names there, UNMOs were deployed in Srebrenica when you were there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- the list at the top of that page is the list of UNMOs who we left in Srebrenica when we departed on the 28th. It's not the list of the UNMOs who were in Srebrenica throughout. Only Mike Beary and for some of the time Ronnie Denuyft were there throughout the time. Trevor Jardins, Fernando Martine -- Martinez, Peter Naglik and David McDonald, were new and had arrived in Srebrenica over the last couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Were you there when Captain McDonald got injured out on his observations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've finished with the diary. There are new areas I can go to. At the same time, a natural sequence would be now to go through the Defence exhibits, many of which we have the difficulty with. So perhaps this would be a good moment to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we made answers clear earlier on this morning. Because of the problem that you touched upon earlier on, and on which I take it the Prosecution is still labouring --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We are. And of course, in the circumstances, we have absolutely no objection to an early adjournment, if that is what Mr. Jones is seeking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But of course -- we have no problem with adjourning either, given the situation as it obtains now. However, I don't want the situation to remain as it is tomorrow morning. In other words, we must report progress on that issue tomorrow morning. Otherwise there will be problems obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Our position is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to reiterate your position, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I told you what the presumption at law is, so please don't force our hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We appreciate the urgency of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry one other thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need the witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. Precisely. In his absence I can make a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel I thank you once more. We will reconvene tomorrow. I think it is in the morning again, 9 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I confirm that I may take the Larry Hollingsworth document with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I would be happy to because I might ask about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Just to say our position on the diary is that only the pages which have been referred to in evidence should be exhibited and not pages which haven't been referred to in evidence. And that's why I've gone through pretty lengthy process of getting confirmation of different points on different pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What about the context in which some of the pages that have been made use of can be understood? You skip pages, for example; so does Mr. Di Fazio. But what is contained in page 10, for example, can only be properly understood if we read also what is on page 9 or on page 11 or on page 20 or on page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well,...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the problem that we have. I mean it's -- plus other things. I mean, I know that strictly speaking, whatever may be contained in the diary which the witness has not been asked to comment about, does not in itself constitute proof of what it says. However, in remote cases sometimes it can constitute corroborative evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I say, Your Honour, I did even before we started I went through every page of the diary and for that reason it's now my position to the whole diary being exhibited. I mean really, it is a matter which I trust the Chamber's wisdom to deal with it as you see fit. It was really just in light of Your Honour's invitation for us to have a position that I put that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate that, Mr. Jones. But you also need to appreciate one thing. For example, if the witness in one page or on one page he says "no distribution as yet of foods or medicine" and on another page, which you may have not referred to says "Distribution has just started", now obviously how do you expect us to ignore that? Now what weight we will give it at the end of the day is our business. But it could constitute corroborative evidence at the end of the time, even if the -- it has not been put to the witness. If witnesses come forward and say something or make an affirmation and they only corroborative evidence that there is may be found in one of pages in this diary, what's the position there?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose -- it does all go to weight and the fact that the witness hasn't confirmed one entry. I would submit makes it of less weight that entries which he has confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously if you want to cut and paste and take as many pages out of this diary from our sight, you are free to do that. It's up to you. But what you leave there we have every right to read if it has been tendered in evidence as one document. I mean, there are other instances where obviously it was not the case, where you stated, We are tendering the entire document, but we are only basically making use of one page and that is what is relevant to this case, and we are ourselves said, Okay, we'll take it that this Trial Chamber will only refer to that page and will ignore completely the rest. That -- of course we'll keep our word there. That's our commitment. But with this particular diary, having -- being familiar with diaries, in this Tribunal and also elsewhere, I know what the difficulty -- where the difficulty lies. It's not as easy as you think. Because a diary has context of its own which starts on day 1 and finishes on day 100 or whichever. And it's difficult to dislodge one extract out of the context in which it happens to be written. The context in time, context of events, temporal. I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, do you want to -- are you finished Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. All of what Your Honour says makes perfect sense and the whole -- so far the whole thing has been exhibited -- well, not the whole thing because there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we don't oppose that. My submissions really go to weight, that matters confirmed by the witness have more weight than those he didn't confirm. I will leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That being the case, the Prosecution would adopt the position that you should admit into evidence the entire document and with respect, we have no problems with the approach that Mr. Jones has suggested, that you may refer to entries upon which this witness has not touched or spoken about, but that you would have to give less weight to those entries because he hasn't explained them, but that you would be permitted and the Prosecution would be permitted and the Defence would be permitted to refer to those particular entries. Now, and that seems, with respect, the simplest way of approaching it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Gentlemen, I can just put one question to the witness and say: Witness, do you confirm, under oath, that there is no false representation in that diary of yours, that everything that is included there reflects the truth of the situation as it was reported to you or as you assessed it, at any given moment? And how does that sound to you, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That sounds fine, if Your Honours please. Don't forget, there is also the evidence that I elicited regarding contemporanaity of the notes, reasonable contemporanaity, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But such a question would actually, then, increase the status and the status of the contents of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially those parts which he is not being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ladies and gentlemen, I want to make myself clear in case -- I wanted to make myself clear, in case anyone may have misunderstood me. When I said I could put that question to the witness, I didn't mean to say that I was going to put that question to the witness. In fact, you can rest assured that it is not my intention to put that question to the witness. If you want to put that question to the witness yourselves, you are free to do so. But not me or any of my two colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I anticipate that the answer from the witness would be quite nuanced in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Yes. No more business to transact today. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00. I think we are sitting in another courtroom tomorrow, or this one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, courtroom 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Courtroom three. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
